claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and picks the best region for each geo.
GeoDeploy is open source in the pulumi/devx-geodeploy GitHub repository.
GeoDeploy's deployment request supports data-residency rules of EU-only, US-only, or in-country.
GeoDeploy's image input specifies platforms amd64, arm64, or both.
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app never makes judgment calls, Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names, and Pulumi never decides anything.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure when enumerating candidate regions.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The post links the Pulumi Automation API to the /automation/ page, which must exist.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the user describes; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only selects from closed sets, so a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction in GeoDeploy.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with the constraints and the image's architecture.
In a single call GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection (choice), five quality scores (score), two hard checks (noul), and a fallback (choice).
The five quality scores are coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, and architecture consistency.
packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the GeoDeploy repo contains buildStageAQuestions using choice, noul, and score imported from @typesafe-ai/sdk.
TypeSafe's advice for writing rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."

GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The TypeSafe SDK exposes TypeSafeClient with a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with selection.choice, confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Weight profiles can be re-tuned in code without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profile values: latency-optimized cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
In GeoDeploy, sprawl risk is subtracted from the composite score, since each extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human choice); region when a stack already exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (use registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (use bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity (drop the AI path for that geo).
packages/decide/src/engine.ts in the GeoDeploy repo contains the residency hard gate check and validation that the selection is a known candidate, throwing AiPathAborted.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`, and periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization.

In self-driving mode GeoDeploy asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate check on disruption risk; code computes node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval, and below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and uses a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates.
Having more choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt; agents can now handle provisioning and day-to-day scaling and reliability decisions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
Jev is a better fit than a general-purpose LLM for infrastructure decisions because it returns typed, confidence-scored answers instead of free text.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Links to /docs/iac/automation-api/ and https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction must resolve.
